stimulus.label: Exhibit A, Reported Emails: Corvel Freight Finance Team
stimulus.context: Two emails reached the Corvel Freight finance team on the same morning. A clerk reported both with the Report button.
stimulus.provenance: Fictional. All organizations, names, and events are invented for assessment purposes only.

email.subject: ACTION REQUIRED: mailbox deleted in 30 minutes
email.body:
Dear user,

Your mailbox failed our security check. It will be DELETED in 30 minutes unless you confirm your password.

Confirm now: https://www.corvelfreight.com/confirm
(the link actually points to https://corvelfreight-support.help/owa/login.php)

Regards,
IT Service Desk

email.subject: Reminder: 41 of your colleagues have already confirmed
email.body:
Hi,

41 people in Finance have already confirmed their accounts today, including your manager. Please don't be the last one.

IT Service Desk

questions.stem: The first email says the mailbox will be deleted in 30 minutes. Which psychological tactic is this mainly using?

choices.text: Reciprocity
Authority of a well-known brand
Liking
Urgency

questions.explanation: A short, frightening deadline is urgency: it pushes the reader to act before they stop and check.

distractor_rationale.A: Reciprocity offers a favour or gift so the victim feels they owe something back; nothing is offered here.
distractor_rationale.B: The sender claims to be IT, but the 30-minute deletion threat, not a brand name, is what drives the reader to act.
distractor_rationale.C: Liking builds rapport or flatters the victim; this email is cold and threatening.

questions.stem: The second email says 41 colleagues, including the reader's manager, have already confirmed. Which tactic does this add?

choices.text: Social proof (consensus)
Intimidation
Scarcity
Pretexting with an insider's name

questions.explanation: Telling the victim that many others have already done it is social proof: people copy what the group seems to be doing.

distractor_rationale.B: Intimidation threatens the victim directly; the reminder is gentle peer pressure instead.
distractor_rationale.C: Scarcity claims something is in short supply (limited offers, last places); nothing is limited here.
distractor_rationale.D: No real insider is named; the email relies on numbers of colleagues, not on a specific trusted person.

questions.stem: Which detail in Exhibit A is the strongest evidence that the link is malicious?

choices.text: The email was sent early in the morning
The email is addressed to a group instead of one person
The visible link shows corvelfreight.com, but it actually goes to corvelfreight-support.help
The subject line uses capital letters

questions.explanation: A link whose real target differs from the text shown is a classic credential-harvesting trick. The real domain, corvelfreight-support.help, is not the company's.

distractor_rationale.A: Send time says little; real staff and attackers both send emails in the morning.
distractor_rationale.B: Group emails are normal for real IT notices too, so this is weak evidence on its own.
distractor_rationale.D: Capital letters suggest pressure but are not proof; the mismatched link target is.

questions.stem: A clerk already clicked the link but has not typed a password. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Forward the email to the whole team as a warning, with the link included
Reply to the sender asking whether the email is genuine
Type a fake password to see what happens
Close the page, report the email, and tell the real IT desk through its known phone number or portal

questions.explanation: Stop, report and verify through a channel you already trust. The real IT desk can block the domain and check whether anything else happened.

distractor_rationale.A: Forwarding the live link spreads the attack; the security team should send a warning without a clickable link.
distractor_rationale.B: Replying goes to the attacker, who will of course say it is genuine.
distractor_rationale.C: Interacting further with an attacker's page can confirm a live target or download more content.

stimulus.label: Exhibit B, Sign-in Log: Corvel Freight Email Accounts
stimulus.context: After the emails in Exhibit A, the security team pulled the sign-in log for the account of finance clerk R. Menon, plus notes on the page she visited.
stimulus.provenance: Fictional. All organizations, names, and events are invented for assessment purposes only.

data.log_name: Corvel Freight, cloud email sign-in log (times IST)

entry.description: R. Menon visited https://corvelfreight-support.help/owa/login.php. The page showed a padlock; its certificate was issued 2 days earlier. The domain was registered 3 days earlier.
The login form on that page sent the typed username and password to corvelfreight-support.help, not to the company's email provider.
Successful sign-in to r.menon@corvelfreight.com from an address in another country on a new device. Password only: the account has no second factor.
New inbox rule created on r.menon's mailbox: move any email containing 'invoice' or 'payment' to the RSS Feeds folder.

questions.stem: Entries N-1 and N-2 describe which kind of attack?

choices.text: Malware installed by a drive-by download
A credential-harvesting page on a look-alike domain
A brute-force attack guessing R. Menon's password
A denial-of-service attack on the email service

questions.explanation: A fake login page on a domain made to look like the company's, which sends the typed password to the attacker, is credential harvesting.

distractor_rationale.A: The page collected a password; no program was downloaded or run.
distractor_rationale.C: No guessing happened: she typed the real password into the fake page.
distractor_rationale.D: Nothing was overloaded or taken offline.

questions.stem: R. Menon says, 'The page had a padlock, so I thought it was safe.' Why was the padlock not enough?

choices.text: A padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site belongs to who it claims to be
Padlocks are only shown when a site has no login form
The padlock proves the page was safe, so the attack must have happened later
The padlock only appears on government websites

questions.explanation: HTTPS encrypts the connection to whatever site you reached. Attackers can get certificates for their own look-alike domains in minutes, as N-1 shows.

distractor_rationale.B: Many genuine and fake login pages show a padlock.
distractor_rationale.C: N-2 shows the password went straight to the attacker's domain from that page.
distractor_rationale.D: Any site can have a padlock, including the attacker's.

questions.stem: What does entry N-4 most likely tell the team?

choices.text: The attacker is hiding payment emails so they can carry out invoice fraud without the clerk noticing
The account has been locked by the provider
The clerk was tidying her inbox
The email provider moved spam automatically

questions.explanation: Rules that hide 'invoice' and 'payment' emails right after an attacker's sign-in are a known business email compromise step: the attacker reads and answers payment emails while the owner can't see them.

distractor_rationale.B: Nothing in the log shows a lock; the attacker is active.
distractor_rationale.C: The rule was made 2 minutes after a foreign sign-in on a new device, not by the clerk.
distractor_rationale.D: Spam filtering doesn't create user inbox rules with these keywords.

questions.stem: Which single control would most likely have stopped the sign-in in N-3, even after the password was stolen?

choices.text: Clearing browser cookies every day
A longer password
Multi-factor authentication, ideally a passkey or security key that only works on the real site
Changing the password every 90 days

questions.explanation: With a second factor, a stolen password alone isn't enough. Phishing-resistant factors such as passkeys go further: they won't work on a look-alike domain at all.

distractor_rationale.A: Clearing cookies on the clerk's PC doesn't stop the attacker signing in from their own device.
distractor_rationale.B: A long password typed into a fake page is stolen just as easily.
distractor_rationale.D: The attacker used the password within 15 minutes; a 90-day change is far too slow.

stimulus.label: Exhibit C, Packet Capture: Hotel Lobby Wi-Fi Lab
stimulus.context: In a classroom lab that copies a hotel lobby, a student ran a packet capture on an open Wi-Fi network while a volunteer used two websites. Two networks with the same name were visible.
stimulus.provenance: Fictional. All organizations, names, and events are invented for assessment purposes only.

data.session:
$ nmcli -f SSID,SIGNAL,SECURITY dev wifi
SSID              SIGNAL  SECURITY
Lobby_Guest       48      WPA2
Lobby_Guest       91      --

$ sudo tcpdump -A -i wlan0 'tcp port 80 or tcp port 443'
10:02:11 IP 10.8.0.23.51522 > 198.51.100.20.80: POST /login HTTP/1.1
    Host: old-forum.example
    username=amaya&password=Sunset2009
10:03:40 IP 10.8.0.23.51530 > 203.0.113.80.443: TLS ClientHello, server name: bank.example
10:03:40 IP 203.0.113.80.443 > 10.8.0.23.51530: TLS ServerHello, Certificate
10:03:41 IP 10.8.0.23.51530 > 203.0.113.80.443: TLS Application Data (encrypted, 1180 bytes)
data.policy_excerpt: Lab rule: captures are made only on the lab network, with the volunteer's consent, and deleted after class.

questions.stem: Why could the student read the volunteer's forum password?

choices.text: The forum login was sent over plain HTTP (port 80), so it was not encrypted
The volunteer's password was too short
tcpdump can decrypt any traffic it captures
The bank website leaked it

questions.explanation: HTTP sends data as plain text, so anyone on the same network who captures packets can read it.

distractor_rationale.B: Password length doesn't matter if the password travels unencrypted.
distractor_rationale.C: The bank traffic in the same capture stayed encrypted; tcpdump can't decrypt TLS by itself.
distractor_rationale.D: The password was sent to old-forum.example, not to the bank.

questions.stem: For the HTTPS connection to bank.example, what could the student still see?

choices.text: Nothing at all, not even the address
Which site was visited (its address and server name) and roughly how much data moved, but not the content
Only the content, but not the website name
The account balance and the password

questions.explanation: TLS hides the content, but the IP address, the server name in the ClientHello, timing and size are still visible to someone watching the network.

distractor_rationale.A: The capture clearly shows the address and server name.
distractor_rationale.C: It's the other way round: the name is visible and the content is hidden.
distractor_rationale.D: The application data is encrypted, as the capture shows.

questions.stem: Two networks are called Lobby_Guest. One has a strong signal and no security. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The hotel installed a faster backup router
An evil twin: someone set up a fake access point with the same name so nearby devices join it
The open network is the hotel's staff network
The laptop's Wi-Fi card is showing the same network twice by mistake

questions.explanation: An open copy of a real network name with a stronger signal is the evil twin pattern: the attacker sits in the middle of everything the victim sends.

distractor_rationale.A: A genuine backup would normally keep the same security settings.
distractor_rationale.C: A staff network would not be open and named for guests.
distractor_rationale.D: The two rows have different security and signal, so they are two different radios.

questions.stem: The volunteer has to use public Wi-Fi tomorrow. Which advice protects them best?

choices.text: Turn off the screen lock so they can work faster
Only use networks with a strong signal
Use incognito mode
Check the exact network name with staff, use only HTTPS sites, and use a trusted VPN; never reuse a password like the forum one

questions.explanation: Confirming the real network defeats the evil twin, HTTPS and a VPN keep traffic encrypted, and unique passwords limit the damage if one leaks.

distractor_rationale.A: A screen lock has nothing to do with network sniffing, and turning it off adds risk.
distractor_rationale.B: The evil twin in Exhibit C had the strongest signal.
distractor_rationale.C: Incognito mode only stops local history; it doesn't encrypt anything on the network.

stimulus.label: Exhibit D, Call Recording and Email: Corvel Freight Accounts Payable
stimulus.context: An accounts payable officer received a call that sounded exactly like the Chief Financial Officer, followed by an email. The CFO often speaks at conferences, and recordings of those talks are online.
stimulus.provenance: Fictional. All organizations, names, and events are invented for assessment purposes only.

data.participants: Caller claiming to be A. Kulkarni (CFO) and S. Fernandes (Accounts Payable)

turn.speaker: Caller
turn.text: Sana, it's Anil. I'm boarding a flight so I can't talk long. We're closing the Halden deal tonight and need to pay their deposit before 7.

turn.speaker: S. Fernandes
turn.text: Of course. Normally I need the approval form for anything over five lakh.

turn.speaker: Caller
turn.text: There's no time for the form. I'm sending the bank details by email now. Keep it quiet until it's announced, okay?

turn.speaker: Email, 17:51
turn.text: From: Anil Kulkarni <a.kulkarni@corvel-freight.co>. 'Sana, as discussed. Great talk at the Mumbai Logistics Summit last month, by the way, the team loved your question on cold-chain delays. Please pay Rs 48,00,000 to the account below by 19:00.'

questions.stem: The voice on the call sounded exactly like the CFO. Which AI-enabled attack is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: A denial-of-service attack on the phone network
A data breach of the payroll system
A computer virus on the officer's phone
A voice deepfake made from recordings of the CFO's public talks

questions.explanation: Voice cloning tools can copy a voice from a few minutes of public audio; the CFO's conference recordings give an attacker exactly that.

distractor_rationale.B: Payroll data isn't involved; the attack asks for a new payment.
distractor_rationale.C: Nothing suggests malware; the attack works on the person, not the device.

questions.stem: The email is fluent, friendly and mentions a real conference question. Why does that no longer prove it is genuine?

choices.text: The email was sent too quickly after the call
Generative AI can write polished, personalised messages from public information such as event recordings and social media
Spelling mistakes are the only reliable sign of phishing
Real executives never mention conferences

questions.explanation: AI tools remove the old warning signs (bad grammar, generic greetings) and can add personal details scraped from public sources.

distractor_rationale.A: Timing alone doesn't prove anything either way.
distractor_rationale.C: Good spelling is now common in phishing, so its absence isn't a reliable sign.
distractor_rationale.D: Real executives might well mention a conference; that is why the detail is convincing.

questions.stem: Which detail in Exhibit D is the clearest technical red flag?

choices.text: The email domain is corvel-freight.co, not the company's corvelfreight.com
The amount is in rupees
The CFO is at an airport
The email thanks the officer for her question

questions.explanation: A look-alike sender domain is hard evidence. The other details are things an attacker can easily fake or that are normal.

distractor_rationale.B: Rupees are normal for an Indian company.
distractor_rationale.C: Travel is a common excuse but not proof.
distractor_rationale.D: The thank-you is social engineering (liking), not a technical indicator.

questions.stem: Which process would best protect the company against this kind of attack in future?

choices.text: Block all phone calls after 17:00
Ask staff to listen carefully for robotic voices
Require every new payee or urgent payment to be confirmed by calling the requester back on a number from the company directory, plus a second approver
Let the CFO approve payments by voice note only

questions.explanation: An out-of-band callback on a known number, plus two-person approval, defeats both a cloned voice and a fake email, however convincing they are.

distractor_rationale.A: Attacks can happen at any time; this blocks real work and doesn't verify anything.
distractor_rationale.B: Good voice clones don't sound robotic; people can't reliably detect them by ear.
distractor_rationale.D: Voice notes can be deepfaked too, so this makes the problem worse.

stimulus.label: Exhibit E, Memo: AI Tools in the Corvel Freight Security Team
stimulus.context: After the incidents in Exhibits A to D, the security lead wrote a memo about two AI tools the company has started using.
stimulus.provenance: Fictional. All organizations, names, and events are invented for assessment purposes only.

memo.subject: How our new AI security tools work, and what they can't do
memo.body:
Team,

(1) The email filter now uses a machine-learning model trained on millions of known phishing and normal emails. Last week it quarantined 212 messages, including both Exhibit A emails.

(2) The sign-in monitor learns each person's normal pattern: usual devices, places and hours. It flagged R. Menon's 08:31 sign-in because the device and country were new for her. It also flagged our CEO three times while she was travelling in Singapore.

(3) A security vendor warns that some attackers now send many low-risk test emails first, to learn what the filter lets through, and then shape their real email to match.

(4) Every flag still goes to an analyst, who decides what happens next. The tools speed us up; they do not replace the payment callback rule or MFA.

Mahesh

questions.stem: How did the sign-in monitor in point (2) decide R. Menon's sign-in was suspicious?

choices.text: It asked her manager
It checked her password against a list of leaked passwords
It read the content of her emails
It compared the sign-in to a learned baseline of her normal devices, places and hours

questions.explanation: This is anomaly detection: the model learns what normal looks like for each user and flags what is far from it.

distractor_rationale.A: The flag came from the tool, not from a person.
distractor_rationale.B: Nothing in the memo mentions leaked-password lists.
distractor_rationale.C: The monitor looks at sign-in details, not email content.

questions.stem: The CEO was flagged three times while travelling. What does this show about the tool?

choices.text: It is broken and should be switched off
Anomaly detection produces false positives when normal behaviour changes, so people must review the flags
The CEO's account was compromised three times
Travel always means an attack

questions.explanation: A real but unusual event, such as a trip, looks like an anomaly. That is a false positive, and it's why point (4) keeps an analyst in the loop.

distractor_rationale.A: False positives are expected; the same tool caught a real compromise.
distractor_rationale.C: The memo explains she was really travelling.
distractor_rationale.D: Most travel is innocent; that is exactly the problem with relying on one signal.

questions.stem: Point (3) describes attackers probing the filter with test emails. What is this an example of?

choices.text: A denial-of-service attack on the email server
Attackers trying to evade an AI model by learning its blind spots
The filter learning from its own mistakes
Normal marketing email

questions.explanation: Adversaries study how a model decides and shape their input to slip past it. This is evasion, and it's why AI defences can't stand alone.

distractor_rationale.A: The emails are low-volume probes, not a flood.
distractor_rationale.C: This is the attacker learning, not the filter.
distractor_rationale.D: The vendor describes deliberate probing by attackers.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up the security lead's position in the memo?

choices.text: AI tools now make MFA and callbacks unnecessary
The email filter should decide on payments automatically
AI tools are too risky and should not be used
AI tools help catch threats faster at scale, but they make mistakes and can be evaded, so they are one layer alongside human review, MFA and payment checks

questions.explanation: The memo shows real benefits (212 quarantined, a real compromise flagged), real limits (false positives, evasion) and keeps other controls: defence in depth.

distractor_rationale.B: The memo keeps decisions with analysts and the payment callback rule.
distractor_rationale.C: The memo says the tools speed the team up and caught real attacks.
